About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Civics, Politics, and Philosophy
Years 12–13 of the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Civics, Politics, and Philosophy Years 12–
13 is still in development. Once that is completed, Civics, Politics, and Philosophy
Years 12–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a National
Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Civics, Politics, and Philosophy Years 12–13 will be required to start using it
in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Civics, Politics, and Philosophy, students explore how societies are governed,
  how citizens participate in public life, and how ideas shape political decisions.
  They study political systems, civic institutions, international relations, global
  citizenship, and philosophical questions about knowledge, ethics, authority,
  freedom, and justice. Through reasoned argument and critical inquiry, students
  learn to evaluate evidence, analyse competing perspectives, and make informed
  judgements about contemporary issues in New Zealand and the wider world.

Students are taught core civic, political, and philosophical concepts and how to
organise knowledge using disciplinary frameworks and systems of thought. Students
explain why argument, evidence, ethical frameworks, political theories, and civic
institutions are important for understanding public life and making informed decisions.

Civics, Politics, and Philosophy provides students with the knowledge and practices
to examine issues, arguments, institutions, and systems in theoretical and real-world
contexts. Students learn to interpret evidence, evaluate competing perspectives,
analyse civic and political processes, and apply philosophical concepts to questions
of knowledge, justice, authority, rights, and power.

As students progress through Years 12–13, they develop the ability to interpret,
analyse, evaluate, and synthesise civic, political, and philosophical information to
make justified judgements and communicate well-reasoned arguments in written
form. This enables them to develop rational arguments that are evidence-based,
ethically informed, and framed by relevant contexts, democratic processes,
competing viewpoints, and the broader social consequences of decisions.

  Civics, Politics, and Philosophy leads to pathways in civics, politics, and
  philosophy and related fields, such as public policy, governance, international
  relations, diplomacy, and law.

 Disciplinary writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In Civics, Politics, and Philosophy, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to explain civic, political, and philosophical concepts; construct and evaluate arguments;
 interpret evidence; compare frameworks, theories, and perspectives; and justify judgements for specific purposes and contexts.

China: one-party socialist state

• The Constitution of the People’s Republic of China declares the National People’s
  Congress (NPC) is the supreme organ of state power that oversees all state
  institutions (president, State Council, Central Military Commission, courts,
  procuratorates).
• The Communist Party of China is defined by its Party Constitution as the
  leadership core of China’s socialist cause. Party leadership directs state organs.
• The State Council is the highest state administrative organ (executive) under a
  premier-responsibility system, operating within the NPC-centred constitutional
  framework.
• The people’s courts and procuratorates are state organs under the Constitution;
  China does not provide for independent constitutional judicial review comparable to
  common-law systems.
• The state structure is unitary and hierarchical, with personnel control and
  supervision mechanisms (e.g. cadre management) ensuring alignment with central
  priorities.
